profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting at a large urban NHS hospital between the qualitative research lead and the acute wards' practice development lead, held one week before fieldwork starts for a study on nurse handover from patient and staff perspectives. The immediate context is that the study will run on two acute medical wards, Cedar and Oak, and requires coordination around ward access, staff briefings, patient information materials, and observation timing without disrupting shift change. The agenda is to align on how the study will be introduced to ward staff, how bedside handovers will be observed, how patient leaflets will be distributed, and what progress can be reported to the upcoming steering group. The expected outcome is a seemingly clear shared plan for starting observations and interviews on both wards and for updating hospital leadership on readiness.

members.name: Dr. Hannah Price
members.expertise: Qualitative health services research, nursing communication, observational fieldwork
members.background: A former acute medical nurse who now leads hospital-based nursing research projects and is responsible for delivering the handover study protocol, including interviews, observations, and ethics compliance.
members.private_state: She wants fieldwork to begin on time so she can show momentum at the steering group meeting, and she is trying to keep the protocol practical enough that ward staff do not feel burdened or become reluctant to participate.
hidden_assumptions: For study purposes, 'bedside handover' includes any nurse-to-nurse transfer of patient information conducted in the patient area, even if the patient is not actively invited into the exchange.
The essential 'team' for briefing is the registered nurses and nurse in charge involved in the observed handovers; HCAs, bank staff, and night staff can be picked up later if needed.
Having both wards 'covered' before the steering group means obtaining enough weekday observation and interview data to show the study is running on each ward, not sampling every shift pattern.
Once the latest patient leaflet is covered by research ethics approval, it is suitable for use on the wards unless someone explicitly flags a local problem.

members.name: Leanne O'Connor
members.role: Practice Development Sister for Acute Medicine
members.expertise: Ward operations, nursing standards, staff education, implementation of bedside handover practices
members.background: An experienced senior nurse overseeing practice improvement across the two acute wards, with responsibility for helping ward teams adopt communication initiatives and for smoothing operational interfaces with audit and research activity.
members.private_state: She wants the study to reflect well on the wards and not generate complaints about confidentiality, exclusion, or disruption, and she is especially alert to anything that might imply one ward is not doing bedside handover 'properly'.
hidden_assumptions: A handover only really counts as 'bedside handover' if it is conducted with the patient present and some degree of patient-facing explanation or involvement.
A 'staff briefing' naturally includes everyone who participates in or shapes handover on the ward, including HCAs, float or bank staff, and night staff.
Saying a ward is 'covered' implies that the study has reached the main shift patterns on that ward so the whole service can fairly be said to have participated.

If a patient-facing leaflet is being used on the ward, any local patient-experience or ward-communications clearance that would be needed has already happened upstream through the research setup process.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they will observe or support 'bedside handover'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means any shift-to-shift exchange about the patient that happens in the patient space or at the bedside area, even if the patient is mostly passive or the nurses keep the conversation minimal.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a more explicit patient-facing bedside handover in which the patient is present as an acknowledged participant, not just nearby while nurses exchange information.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using accepted language from nursing practice and policy, and each interpretation sounds normal enough that neither expects the term to need unpacking in a short coordination meeting.

misalignment_points.topic: Who is included in the team briefing
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'brief the team at handover' before observations begin.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means the registered nurses and nurse in charge on the shifts she plans to observe first, since they are the core participants in the study's initial handover observations.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes the wider handover ecosystem on both wards, such as HCAs, bank staff, and night staff, because they affect how handover is experienced and who is present at the bedside.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ward life, 'the team' is a routine umbrella phrase, and both speakers are being cooperative, so each hears the phrase as naturally matching their own operational boundary.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to have both wards covered
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the study should have 'covered both wards' before the steering group update.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means she has enough initial observation periods and a small number of interviews on each ward to demonstrate that fieldwork is underway and yielding usable data.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the study has reached the main shift patterns on each ward, including at least some night or out-of-hours activity, so no subgroup feels overlooked and the ward can say participation was service-wide.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Coverage is being used as a progress shorthand rather than a formal metric, and in a coordination discussion it sounds like a harmless shared milestone rather than something requiring exact sampling criteria.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to using 'the approved patient leaflet' for introducing the study.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the REC-approved current leaflet can simply be taken onto the ward and handed out by the research team before observed handovers.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes that if the leaflet is approved, any local patient-experience and ward-facing wording issues have already been cleared, including its use in routine bedside distribution.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Approval pathways are usually handled in separate governance streams, so each person treats their own part of the process as the invisible default and hears 'approved' as confirming that everything upstream is settled.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to sound tidy and ready to go. If I can start on Cedar next week and get enough observation sessions and a few interviews on both wards before the steering group, that is plenty to show momentum. I do not need every shift pattern yet; I just need to be able to say both wards are covered and fieldwork has begun without making this feel heavy for staff.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time, Leanne. I just wanted to line up the last practical bits for starting on Cedar and Oak next week, so I can give the steering group a clear update and say we’ve covered both wards as the study gets underway.

turns.inner_thought: The wards know something is coming, but I want nobody saying later that people were left out or not told. If we put a short message into handover, that can reach the whole ward ecosystem, including the staff who are around handover but are often missed. That should also help this land as supportive rather than intrusive.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. Both wards are expecting the study, and the easiest thing will probably be to brief the team at handover so everyone knows what’s happening before you start.

turns.inner_thought: Good, a brief word at handover should be enough for the registered nurses and nurse in charge on the late shift I’m starting with. I’m planning to begin on Cedar late shift and then observe bedside handover in the patient areas. I don’t need a big all-staff rollout before I can get going.
turns.utterance: That would work really well. I’m planning to start with the late shift on Cedar, and if I can observe bedside handover after the team has had that introduction, that should let us get moving smoothly.

turns.inner_thought: Cedar has made more effort recently to do bedside handover in a visible, patient-facing way, whereas Oak still often starts with a nurse-in-charge piece away from the bedside. Still, I don’t want this framed as one ward doing it right and one doing it wrong. Better to reassure her both wards can support the study.
turns.utterance: That should be fine. Cedar’s been trying to make bedside handover a bit more visible on the bays, and Oak still tends to do a nurse-in-charge piece first, but both wards should be absolutely workable for the study.

turns.inner_thought: As long as I can get a foothold on each ward before the steering group, I’m happy. A handful of weekday sessions and some early interviews will let me say the observational phase is properly underway. I should keep the language broad so everyone feels progress is being made.
turns.utterance: Perfect. If I can get both wards covered before the steering group, I’ll feel comfortable saying the observational phase is properly underway.

turns.inner_thought: Covered needs to mean the main shift patterns, otherwise nights or out-of-hours staff will say the study only saw one slice of ward life. I’d rather set that expectation now, but without making it sound like I’m complicating things. If she can touch early, late, and night, I can stand behind it with matrons.
turns.utterance: Yes, agreed. Coverage across the early, late and night patterns will help as well, just so there’s no sense that one part of the ward routine was missed.

turns.inner_thought: I’ll bring the REC-approved leaflet and leave copies with the nurses I’m shadowing. That should be enough for introducing the study before observed handovers. I’m assuming if the leaflet is approved, it’s fine to use unless someone tells me there’s a local issue. No need to open up another governance track a week before starting.
turns.utterance: That sounds sensible. I’ll bring the approved patient leaflet and leave packs for the nurses I’m shadowing, so patients can be informed ahead of the observation period.

turns.inner_thought: Good, if it’s the approved patient leaflet then all the local wording and patient-experience angles should already have been dealt with in setup. We can keep copies on the ward and use them routinely if someone asks what the study is about. That will make this easier operationally.
turns.utterance: Yes, that’s fine. If it’s the approved patient leaflet, we can keep copies on the ward side as well for routine use if needed.

turns.inner_thought: I should make sure the key people on the shifts I’m observing understand the study and how to introduce patient involvement without overcomplicating it. Mainly I need the nurse in charge and the receiving nurses ready for what I’ll be doing around bedside handover. I don’t need to brief every role in detail before starting.
turns.utterance: And just so it’s manageable, in that initial briefing I mainly want the nurse in charge and the receiving nurses to understand the study purpose and how patient involvement in bedside handover will be explained.

turns.inner_thought: I hear her, but I still need everyone around handover to know what this is, otherwise HCAs, bank staff or nights will feel bypassed and that’s when concerns come in. They all shape whether bedside handover feels appropriate and confidential. I’ll make sure the whole team gets the message without making a fuss.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. I’ll make sure the whole team hears about it, including HCAs and whoever is on nights, because they all shape how handover feels at the bedside.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds supportive. By the end of next week, if I’ve done Cedar late shifts and at least started Oak, I should be able to tell the steering group both wards are covered and bedside handover observations are in progress. That’s the key message: active fieldwork, not delay.
turns.utterance: Great. So after next week, I’m hoping to be able to say both wards are covered and that bedside handover observations are in progress on the acute medicine side.

turns.inner_thought: Fine. I’ll arrange a briefing through handover, get the leaflet visible on both wards, and tell matrons the study is on track. From my side, that means the wider team is aware, the approved leaflet is in circulation, and we’re moving toward proper ward-wide coverage. That should protect the wards if questions come up.
turns.utterance: That sounds like a good plan. I’ll slot the briefing into handover, circulate the leaflet on the wards, and let the matrons know the study is on track.
